context: a letter from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
I am extremely puzzled how to advise about Scott. As a rule in such cases the “least said the soonest mended,” I wish to Heavens I had asked Balfour before— you must not on any account let him know of our having had any communication with Balfour. he would put B. down as his enemy at once & there might be the devil to pay.— You cannot conceive what trouble men of Scotts temperament give us. One is now threatening us with an action for not giving him a good enough character, on this very ground of sulky pig-headed celtic disposition. A capital young gardener he is too—clever, well informed, & an excellent worker— the wretch has cost me hours of time & thought, advice & warning—all to no purpose   he is very grateful to me personally & has not given me a word of offence, nor anything but thanks for my efforts to reform him—but I have not moved him one inch to better courses, & his conduct has been disgraceful. & after kicking up a precious row, he leaves us with a threat.— Then again pray consider (what we often have to) if you do take & employ him for 2 years, what is he to do after that?—when he will have lost much of his utilitarian gardening skill. I hope the poor fellow is not married.

Do pray take care, of all classes of men Gardeners are the most troublesome I ever had dealings with—what with their superficial knowlged, tempers, the conflict of science & practice in their brains, conceit & tyrannical conduct to those under them— they do require very careful treatment.

My dear friend this is a wretched letter to send you.— I will not cease to think if anything could possibly turn up for Scott— The only thing I can think of is a Nursery Garden of his own, but then he would never make it pay!

Ever yrs affec | J D Hooker.

Rolleston wrote the Review of Schleiden

Cordial thanks for your excellent advice about Scott.— I have written to him, merely saying that I know that you wd. aid him, if in your power; but that he must not in the least trust to this in looking to the future; that you had men of your own to recommend, & that you did not know him personally.— I see there is no help, but it is really a pity that an indomitable worker shd. not be able to follow out laborious researches, which no one else will probably for years undertake. Again I thank you sincerely.— I have asked Scott to tell me his plans

When you write to Chief Baron, pray thank him with my sincere respect for his kind enquiries after me.— I really begin to hope that I shall recover & work again— Dr. Jenner has done me much good & is, I am sure, a most able doctor: drinking very little—enormous quantities of chalk, magnesia & Carb. of Ammonia has checked the vomiting wonderfully & I am gaining vigour. I can now read a very little & am beginning a sort of work, (not exciting!) viz counting the seeds in capsules of Lythrum. I believe in a fortnight, if I do not go back, I shall dictate my paper on Lythrum!!!!—

I have been wonderfully interested by Oliver’s paper on Dimorphic flowers which has been read to me— How I shd like to cultivate Leersia— Could I grow it in a large shallow tub? Have you seed? Could you tell me any Botanist in Sussex or Hampshire to whom I could write & who could send me plants? or is it hopeless?— That the perfect flowers shd. not be fertile is wondrous, & I shd. like to examine into the case.— I am educating my under gardener into an expert experimentalist.—

Farewell my dear & best of old friends | Ever yours affect | C. Darwin
